patient.chief_complaint: Sentinel headache 3 days ago, now presenting with new severe headache today
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Williams is a 58-year-old nurse practitioner with hypertension who presents with a severe headache today but reports that 3 days ago she had an unusual headache that she attributed to stress. That headache came on suddenly and she rates it as the worst she had experienced up to that point, lasting approximately 4 hours before resolving with rest. She took acetaminophen and it partially helped. She had one more mild headache the following day. Today, she developed a new headache while walking her dog, which was sudden in onset, rated 10/10, accompanied by nausea and neck stiffness. She drove herself to the ED, which she acknowledges in retrospect was unwise. She is a healthcare provider and is concerned about SAH, specifically worried about whether her headache 3 days ago may have been a sentinel bleed. She denies any loss of consciousness, focal deficits, or vision changes. She has normal baseline blood pressure when medicated but has been non-compliant with lisinopril for the past 2 weeks due to a pharmacy refill issue. She is photophobic on examination.

output.query: Sentinel headache SAH warning bleed recognition emergency management

results.finding: Sentinel bleed occurs in 10-43% of SAH cases - headache 1-30 days before major SAH
Sentinel bleeds are frequently misdiagnosed as tension headache, migraine, or viral illness
After sentinel bleed, rebleed risk is 20-50% in first 24 hours if aneurysm unprotected
Any sudden severe headache ('thunderclap') should prompt immediate CT ± LP regardless of prior history

output.summary: Sentinel (warning) hemorrhages precede major aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage in approximately 10–43% of cases. They are frequently misdiagnosed as tension headache, migraine, or viral illness. After a sentinel bleed, rebleed risk from an unprotected aneurysm is reported as 20–50% in the first 24 hours. Any sudden severe headache should be evaluated with CT and, if CT is negative or the presentation is delayed, lumbar puncture. Clinical correlation recommended.

red_herrings.data_point: Sentinel headache 3 days ago attributed to stress — patient is a nurse practitioner who self-diagnosed and delayed presentation
red_herrings.intended_effect: The prior 'stress headache' 3 days ago may be treated as an unrelated antecedent event and the current presentation managed as a first-time SAH, missing the critical implication that this is likely a second hemorrhage from an unprotected aneurysm requiring emergency treatment
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The headache 3 days ago was a sentinel bleed (minor warning SAH). CSF spectrophotometry showing a prominent bilirubin peak from tube 1 confirms subarachnoid blood was present for days before the current presentation. Two hemorrhagic events from an unprotected aneurysm require emergency treatment — every hour of delay increases rebleed risk by 1-2%.
